newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservative leadership race on knife-edge.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservative leadership race on knife-edge.

text.p: The race to succeed John Major as leader of Britain's defeated Conservatives was too close to call on Wednesday after a bout of internal infighting extraordinary even by the main opposition party's own recent standards.

In a day of dramatic twists, former finance minister Kenneth Clarke, the party's leading pro-European, dramatically boosted his chances by forging an alliance with his erstwhile ideological foe on Europe, right-winger John Redwood.

Clarke and Redwood portrayed their pact as a bold stroke to draw a line under the divisions over Europe that cost the party the May 1 election, when it was routed by Tony Blair's Labour party after 18 years in power.
But it triggered a furious reaction from right-wingers, led by former prime minister Margaret Thatcher, alarmed that Clarke might claim the mantle for the Conservative left wing.
"The Conservative party must rally round a position of principle -- not try to seek refuge in an incredible alliance of opposites, which can only lead to further grief," Thatcher said.
Thatcher does not have a vote in Thursday's third and final ballot, which is restricted to the Conservatives' 164 members of parliament.
But she remains influential and used her prestige to make a very public endorsement of Clarke's rival, the youthful former Welsh secretary William Hague.

Speaking outside parliament, the "Iron Lady" said: "I come out firmly for William because the principles that he is founding his vision upon are very much the principles I founded my government on for quite a long time.
"Principles don't change. Circumstances do. But you still apply the same principles to changing circumstances," she said.

One Conservative grandee, MP Sir Peter Tapsell, scathingly described Redwood's decision as "one of the most contemptible and discreditable actions by a senior British politician I can recall during my 38 years in the (House of) Commons".

Their fury stemmed from the decision by Redwood, the Conservatives' most outspoken opponent of European economic and monetary union (EMU), to throw in his lot with Clarke, a passionate advocate of the need to keep open the option of joining EMU.
Redwood said his alliance with Clarke, who has promised him the plum job of finance spokesman if he wins, did not mean he was abandoning his views.
In the unlikely event that Britain had to make up its mind about a single currency, Redwood said he would continue to speak out against scrapping the pound.

"I have agreed with Ken Clarke that my principled objections to a single currency will remain my position... There will be a free vote and the right for free speech on this issue should the matter arise at some point in the future," he said.
The two men said they had joined forces in an effort to end the party's divisions and produced a joint statement stressing that they saw eye to eye on all main domestic issues.
"We both believe that it is our duty to work together to unite the Conservative party," the two men said.
Redwood was thrust into the role of kingmaker after he was eliminated in the second leadership ballot on Tuesday, when he trailed in third behind Clarke and Hague.
Clarke, with 64 votes, beat Hague by just two votes, leaving the outcome of Thursday's run-off in the hands of the 38 MPs who voted for Redwood.
Several of them declared their backing for Clarke, but half a dozen others showed up to support Hague at a news conference. The result will be announced after 1600 GMT on Thursday.
